title: Learning from different generations
transcript:
Hi Georgie.
Hi Phil.
So, Georgie, do you often spend time with people who are much older than you or much younger than you?
I do, actually, because I'm in a choir, so there's quite a wide range of ages – lots of older people, lots of younger people.
We can call an age group of people a generation. And you might feel that it's difficult to understand or agree with people from a different generation. Today on 6 Minute English, we're going to be finding out about a project that is gathering together the oldest people – that's those that are retired – with the youngest, and that's children who attend nursery. And we'll be asking the question, 'What can we learn from different generations?'
Let's start with our quiz question, Georgie. What generation would someone born in 1982 be in? Is it: a) Generation X, b) Millennial, or c) Gen Z.
Phil, I'm going to go with Generation X.
OK. Well, we will find out the answer at the end of the programme.
OK. Phil, so you said we're going to look at a project which gets small children interacting with older retired people. So, how does it work?
Well, in Chester, in the northwest of England, a nursery has opened up in a retirement village. There's the usual nursery staff to look after the children, but the older residents can join in for activities as well. There's a library, a cafeteria and a garden for the children and the older people to share, and some of the older people or 'grand-friends', as the children call them, lead some of the activities, like dance or crafts. And presenter of BBC World Service podcast People Fixing the World, Myra Anubi, went to visit the special nursery and spoke to some of the participants.
Ian was once a fighter pilot, and getting involved in the nursery has helped him fill a void.
It was after my wife died last year. It seemed I had a big, big hole to fill. And the people down in the nursery, they phoned me up and said, "We were doing such and such a thing. Why don't you come and join us?" And that's what I've been doing. So, yes, and I've enjoyed it. And I find it very interesting to see how they develop.
One of the things I heard from the grapevine is that you help the children make paper planes.
That's right.
Myra says that the nursery helped Ian fill a void after his wife sadly died. If you fill a void, you find something to help you feel better after a loss.
Ian explains that after his wife died, staff at the nursery would phone him to tell him about the daily activities, which he refers to as such and such. And that's an expression that we use to talk about something without giving a specific example.
It sounds like Ian has enjoyed spending time with the children at the nursery, and Myra tells him she's heard from the grapevine that he's been teaching the children to make paper planes.
Yes, hear from the grapevine is an expression, meaning that something is a rumour. And we also say, hear on the grapevine.
Well, this nursery sounds like a really lovely project, Phil. What is the impact it's having on the older and younger people?
Well, the charity Ready Generations, which runs the nursery, says it works with universities to study the effects of mixing generations on health and wellbeing, and they say they've seen positive results. And there have been studies around the world on projects that encourage different generations to mix, and they found that they can help reduce loneliness, improve how healthy and well people feel, and even boost learning and creativity. People Fixing the World host Myra spoke to Liz Ludden, co-founder of the nursery in Chester, about the differences that she's noticed since it opened.
And as I realised, these interactions also seem to be breaking down stereotypes.
Your first thought would be how lively and energetic young children can be, and what we found is so can older people. And so sometimes, you know, it's the older people that we're saying, "Can we just calm this down a little bit?"
Myra says the nursery breaks down stereotypes. This means it provides evidence that common beliefs about a group of people are not true.
For example, a stereotype about generations is that younger people are lively, meaning they're loud and have lots of energy, whereas older people are not that lively.
Right. But in the nursery, Liz says it's often the older people who have lots of energy and are being noisy rather than the children. The staff even have to tell them to calm down sometimes!
So, Georgie, is that something that you found in your choir?
Actually, yes. The older people in my choir are big characters. It's often them who are dragging us all to the pub...!
OK. Georgie, I think it's time to look at the answer for that question. I asked if someone was born in 1982, which generation would they be from?
I said Generation X.
OK. Well, actually, I'm afraid the answer was b) – they're a Millennial, just like you!
Ah...! OK. Let's recap the vocabulary we learned in this programme, starting with generation, which is a group of people who are of a similar age.
Fill a void means find something to help you feel better after experiencing loss.
Such and such is a way to talk about something without giving a specific example.
If you hear something on the grapevine, you hear a rumour.
The expression break down stereotypes means find evidence that common beliefs about a group of people are untrue.
And lively means loud and with lots of energy.
Once again, our six minutes are up, but you can test what you've learned with the worksheet on our website. Go to bbclearningenglish.com.
Thanks for joining us and goodbye.
Goodbye!

context_glossary.grandfriends: 祖辈朋友（孩子对老人的称呼）

sentences.text: Hi Georgie.
sentences.translation: 嗨，乔治。

sentences.text: Hi Phil.
sentences.translation: 嗨，菲尔。

sentences.text: So, Georgie, do you often spend time with people who are much older than you or much younger than you?
sentences.translation: 那么，乔治，你经常和比你大很多或小很多的人相处吗？

sentences.text: I do, actually, because I'm in a choir,
sentences.translation: 其实有的，因为我在一个合唱团里，

sentences.text: so there's quite a wide range of ages – lots of older people,
sentences.translation: 所以团里年龄跨度挺大的——有很多年纪大的，

sentences.text: lots of younger people.
sentences.translation: 也有很多年轻人。

sentences.text: We can call an age group of people a generation.
sentences.translation: 我们可以把一个年龄段的人群称为一代人。

sentences.text: And you might feel that it's difficult to understand or agree with people from a different generation.
sentences.translation: 你可能会觉得很难理解或认同其他世代的人。

sentences.text: Today on 6 Minute English,

sentences.text: we're going to be finding out about a project that is gathering together the oldest people – that's those that are retired – with the youngest,
sentences.translation: 我们要了解一个把最年长的人——也就是退休的人——和最年幼的人

sentences.text: and that's children who attend nursery.
sentences.translation: 也就是上托儿所的孩子聚在一起的项目。

sentences.text: And we'll be asking the question,
sentences.translation: 我们还会探讨一个问题：

sentences.text: 'What can we learn from different generations?'
sentences.translation: '我们能从不同世代的人身上学到什么？'

sentences.text: Let's start with our quiz question, Georgie.
sentences.translation: 乔治，我们先用一个问题开始今天的测验。

sentences.text: What generation would someone born in 1982 be in?
sentences.translation: 1982年出生的人属于哪一代？

sentences.text: Is it: a) Generation X,
sentences.translation: 是：a) X世代，

sentences.text: b) Millennial, or c) Gen Z.
sentences.translation: b) 千禧一代，还是 c) Z世代？

sentences.text: Phil, I'm going to go with Generation X.
sentences.translation: 菲尔，我选X世代。

sentences.text: OK.
sentences.translation: 好。

sentences.text: Well, we will find out the answer at the end of the programme.
sentences.translation: 我们会在节目最后揭晓答案。

sentences.text: OK.
sentences.translation: 好的。

sentences.translation: 菲尔，你刚才说要介绍一个让小孩与退休老人互动的项目。

sentences.text: So, how does it work?
sentences.translation: 那它是怎么运作的呢？

sentences.text: Well, in Chester, in the northwest of England,
sentences.translation: 嗯，在英格兰西北部的切斯特，

sentences.text: a nursery has opened up in a retirement village.
sentences.translation: 一个托儿所在退休村里开了起来。

sentences.text: There's the usual nursery staff to look after the children,
sentences.translation: 有 usual 的托儿所员工照看孩子，

sentences.text: but the older residents can join in for activities as well.
sentences.translation: 但年长的居民也可以参加活动。

sentences.text: There's a library, a cafeteria and a garden for the children and the older people to share,
sentences.translation: 有一个图书馆、一间咖啡馆和一个花园，供孩子和老人共享，

sentences.text: and some of the older people or 'grand-friends',
sentences.translation: 有些老人，或者孩子们称呼的'祖辈朋友'，

sentences.text: as the children call them,
sentences.translation: 就像孩子们叫他们那样，

sentences.text: lead some of the activities,
sentences.translation: 会主持一些活动，

sentences.text: like dance or crafts.
sentences.translation: 比如跳舞或手工。

sentences.translation: BBC世界服务播客《人类修复世界》的主持人

sentences.translation: 参与托儿所活动帮助他填补了内心的空虚。

sentences.translation: 就是听到了传闻。

sentences.text: The expression break down stereotypes means find evidence that common beliefs about a group of people are untrue.
sentences.translation: break down stereotypes（打破刻板印象）指找到证据证明对某群体的普遍看法不属实。

sentences.text: And lively means loud and with lots of energy.
sentences.translation: lively（活泼）指爱热闹、精力充沛。

sentences.text: Once again, our six minutes are up,
sentences.translation: 又到了节目结束的时间，

sentences.text: but you can test what you've learned with the worksheet on our website.
sentences.translation: 但你可以在我们网站的练习册上测试所学内容。

sentences.text: Go to bbclearningenglish.com.
sentences.translation: 访问 bbclearningenglish.com。

sentences.text: Thanks for joining us and goodbye.
sentences.translation: 感谢收听，再见。

sentences.text: Goodbye!
sentences.translation: 再见！
